title: The Godfather Part II
synopsis: A young Vito in New York, a cold Michael in Nevada, and a family that does not survive its own success.

nodes.text: Tahoe. A band on the lawn, a boy in a white suit who did not want the party, three hundred people eating your food. Inside, the senator sits in your study and tells you what he thinks of your family and your kind while a fee is being negotiated. He wants a hundred thousand a quarter, in cash, by hand. You let him finish. You have learned to let men finish.

choices.consequence: You offer him nothing at all, in exactly the tone he used for the insult, and watch his mouth work. It is the most enjoyable half-minute of your decade.
You put a number on the desk and he picks it up. Owning a man is cheaper than beating one and does not require you to remember his face.

nodes.text: Two men, curtains open, the bed the obvious target from the water. Glass goes across the rug in the exact shape of the window. Kay is down on the floor in the dark with her arms over her head and the baby crying at the end of the hall. The shooters turn up in the boathouse before dawn, dead, which tells you they were never getting off the property either.

choices.consequence: You start with your own house, room by room, and write the list of people who knew which bedroom was yours. The list is short and every name on it is family.
You put your wife and children in a car at four in the morning without saying where it is going. She asks. You tell her it's handled. That is the last conversation for months.

nodes.text: Frankie comes out to the desert in a bad jacket, complains about the wine, insults the band, and asks your permission to bury the Rosato brothers, who are taking his neighbourhoods one block at a time. He is loyal and old and loud and he asks you with waiters in the room. Roth needs him breathing for the moment. So, for the moment, he breathes.

choices.consequence: You tell him to keep his territories and do nothing, and you mean the second half of that. You are setting a man out where somebody else can reach him.
You give him no answer whatsoever and let him drive back to Brooklyn carrying it. Frankie has never once in his life been able to sit quietly with silence.

nodes.text: A bungalow, a card table, a tuna sandwich, a ballgame on the television with the sound off. Roth is old and gentle and cuts you a slice of cake with a country's name iced across it. Havana, the hotels, the new arrangement, the arithmetic. Then he mentions Moe Greene, and how nobody ever asked who had ordered it. He says it warmly. He wants you to hear both halves.

choices.consequence: You eat the cake and agree with everything. He has just told you he knows. You have just told him you know he knows. Neither sentence was spoken.
You lean on the Havana figures once, only to see what he does under pressure. He coughs, apologizes, and produces a number that was ready before you sat down.

nodes.text: The palace, gold telephones handed out as party favours, assurances that the rebels will be finished before Easter. Then a captured boy pulls a pin in the back of a police car and takes an officer with him, and you watch it through glass and know the money is already gone. At midnight the balloons come down. You take Fredo's face in both hands and say it in front of everyone.

choices.consequence: You get out of the country in the confusion with two million still uncommitted. Roth leaves on a stretcher and survives it. You do not regard that as luck.
You leave before the toast, which is an insult that will be reported upward. You have stopped caring how you look to men who will be dead or exiled by March.

nodes.text: He gave it to you in front of the fireworks without knowing he had. Johnny Ola. The girl at the hotel. A favour nobody had ever asked him for before, and he was so pleased to have been asked. Now he stands in the noise with his hands out, explaining that he is the older one, that he was passed over, that he has been stepped around for thirty-eight years.

choices.consequence: You hold him against you where the whole party can see it and put your mouth beside his ear. They see a brother. Fredo feels the temperature and starts shaking.
You decide he lives as long as your mother does. That is not mercy. It is a date written into a book, and you are the one who keeps the book.

nodes.text: Nineteen seventeen, a basement on Mott Street, a hand-cranked olive press and one bare bulb on a cord. Your name is Vito, you are twenty-five, your wife is upstairs and your boy is in the crib. Clemenza asks you to hide guns in your ceiling and afterward gives you a rug that is not his to give. Then Fanucci's men come by to explain the neighbourhood's arrangements.

choices.consequence: You say the wrong quiet thing to the wrong man, and by the end of the week every doorway on the block knows your face. Fanucci raises the figure for the insult.
You hand over what you are told to hand over, then climb the stairs and sit at the table with your wife doing sums on paper that will not come out right.

nodes.text: Festa night, the street lit from end to end, a plaster saint carried past on shoulders with banknotes pinned all over his robes. The man in the white suit walks home heavy with wine, hat in hand, humming. You go over the rooftops with a towel wound around the pistol. He gets his key into the lock. You are already on the stairs behind him when he turns.

choices.consequence: Three, close in, the last one through the mouth so the street understands the message without anyone having to explain it. Then home over the roofs, to kiss your son.
You spend one round more than you intended and finish it in a way that keeps you sitting on those stairs a moment longer than planned. The calm on the walk home unsettles you.

nodes.text: Washington. Flashbulbs, a bench of microphones, your attorney at your elbow and Kay seated behind you in a hat she bought for the occasion. A senator reads aloud a list of the things you are alleged to be, and mispronounces two of them. Your statement asks that your war record be entered into the record. You read it flat. Every reporter present writes down that you were calm.

choices.consequence: You answer four questions and decline the rest on advice. The papers run the refusals in a column with your photograph, which is precisely what the committee came for.
You give them dates and a decoration and invite them to call you a liar on camera. They adjourn instead, and go out and find themselves a witness.

nodes.text: The witness is sworn and has your entire life typed on the pages in front of him. Then the doors open at the back and an old man in a black hat is walked in and seated in the second row: Vincenzo Pentangeli, off a plane from Sicily, who has not spoken to his brother in twenty years. Frankie turns around. Frankie looks. Frankie starts saying he was mistaken.

choices.consequence: You put the brother where Frankie cannot avoid seeing the hat, and nobody says a word to anybody. The old country does the rest of the work for free.
You keep the old man out of the gallery and let Frankie sweat through one more morning first. Pressure works better when nobody in the room can name what it is.

nodes.text: The hotel suite after the hearings. You tell her it is finished and you are taking everyone home. She says she isn't going anywhere with you. Then she says it about the miscarriage: that it wasn't one, that it was a decision, that it was a son, and that she did it so that this would stop with you. She says it steadily and does not look away once.

choices.consequence: Your hand moves before any part of you agrees to it. The sound is small in a large room. Every wall you built between the two halves of your life comes down in one motion.
You put her out of your family in a level voice and leave without slamming anything at all. Cold is worse than shouting, and both of you understand that perfectly.

nodes.text: Tom comes down to the boathouse with the news. Frankie is finished, the government has him in an army barracks behind wire, and he has worked out what the old arrangements really were. In the Roman days, Tom says, a man who backed the losing side could go home, open his veins in a warm bath, and his family kept everything. He offers it as history. You let him finish saying it.

choices.consequence: You nod once and Tom drives off to deliver a history lesson in a bathhouse. Frankie's people keep the house in New Jersey and are never told the reason why.
You consider stopping it for about the length of a cigarette, on the grounds that Frankie once carried your father up a staircase. Then you finish the cigarette.

nodes.text: You come back at forty with a good coat and an American passport, and Tommasino drives you up the hill to the courtyard. Don Ciccio is blind now and asks whose son you are. Your mother died on a road below this house with a knife at her throat, bargaining for a boy. You lean in close enough that the old man can feel your breath, and you give him the name.

choices.consequence: You say your father, your brother, your mother, then yourself, in that order, close to his ear. Then one motion finishes what a nine-year-old started on a mountain.
You say almost nothing and let the blade carry the sentence. Riding down the hill you feel nothing whatsoever, and you never tell your wife where you have been.

nodes.text: Carmela is carried out by men who have killed for this family, all of them in their good suits, all of them steady. Connie sits in black at the front. Fredo hangs at the back, unsure whether he is permitted to be in the building. Connie takes your arm and asks you to do this for her, here, with your mother in front of you. You cross the aisle.

choices.consequence: You hold him where the whole church can see it and let him cry into your shoulder. Over his back you find Neri's eyes and hold them a beat too long.
You embrace him because your sister asked and your mother is in the box. Nothing gets forgiven. A clock is wound, and set down, and left ticking.

nodes.text: She comes back from Europe without the man in the sports car: thin, sober, apologetic in a register you have never heard from her. She says she spent years hurting you on purpose because you took her husband. She asks for a room and something useful to do and the children to look after. You give her both. She has decided you are all that remains, and she is not far wrong.

choices.consequence: You hand her the running of the house and she is good at it, and soon she is bringing you cardigans and appointments. You now have one ally and no equals left anywhere.
You make her wait four days for an answer she was always going to get. Making people wait is how you learn what they will still do for you afterward.

nodes.text: Israel has refused him. Argentina, Panama, Venezuela, all refused. Sixty-seven years old with a heart that is finishing him anyway, coming down the aircraft steps in Miami into a wall of reporters and federal marshals with the newsreels running. Six months, the doctors say. Nobody at your table understands why you want it done there, in public, in front of cameras, at that price.

choices.consequence: You send Rocco through the press pack with a reporter's credential and a small pistol. Rocco does not come back out of the terminal. You knew that and sent him anyway.
You set it aside for an afternoon and price out simply letting the heart finish him. Then you decide that a man who dies in a bed is a man who beat you.

nodes.text: He has been taking your son out on the lake, teaching him the fishing and the old prayer that is supposed to bring them up. The boy is in Reno with his mother now, which you arranged on Tuesday. Fredo goes out at dusk because you told him to go, and Neri sits behind him with a shotgun under the seat, and Fredo is saying a Hail Mary for the fish.

choices.consequence: You give the nod in the kitchen without setting your glass down. It takes under a second. You spend the remaining years of your life not thinking about it on purpose.
You hold it until the light is gone and the boy is forty miles off. You have become a man who weighs the timing of a thing more carefully than the thing itself.

nodes.text: She comes on the arranged Saturday and the children go down the hall at a run. Anthony will not look up at you. Mary puts her face into her mother's coat. Kay stands in the doorway of a house she used to live in, holding her handbag in front of her like something to get behind, and you watch from the landing and count off the minutes she has been allowed.

choices.consequence: You come down and put your hand flat on the door and push it shut while she is still saying her son's name. You keep the sound of that for the rest of your life.
You let the visit run its full hour and stay upstairs so she never has to speak to you. Generosity costs you nothing now, and it purchases nothing either.

nodes.text: December, nineteen forty-one, the dining room on Mott Street laid for the old man's birthday with everybody home. Sonny loud with a girl on his arm, Tessio carrying the cake in, Fredo the only one who reaches over and shakes your hand when you tell them you enlisted. Then the cars pull up outside and the whole table stands and goes out into the hall to meet your father.

choices.consequence: You take Sonny calling you a chump, and Tom's lecture about the scholarship, and you smile through all of it, because you already signed and none of them can undo a signature.
You stay in the chair while the family shouts its welcome in the hallway, alone with the candles and the empty places. That is where the memory always stops.

nodes.text: The water is flat and grey and there is a small boat out past the point with nobody standing up in it. You watch from the window with a glass in your hand and you do not go down to the shore. The gulls settle again. Somebody will bring the boat in this afternoon, and no one in this house will ask a single question about it, today or ever.

choices.consequence: You sit down by the glass and stay there while the light comes up across the lake. When it goes again in the evening you do not turn on the lamp.
You turn from the window and go back into a house containing a sister, a housekeeper, two children in Reno, and not one person you could say this to.

nodes.text: The room is heated and dusted and nobody enters it without knocking twice. A leather chair, a desk with nothing on it, and on the side table a small photograph of your father at thirty, squinting outside the shop with his sleeves rolled. The door to the hall is standing wide open. You could walk out of it. You have been able to walk out of it for years.

choices.consequence: You take the chair, because the chair is what there is. Everything you own is visible from this room and not one item in it will speak to you.
You stay on your feet by the window like a man who is about to leave, which is something you have done every evening for years without ever leaving.
You do neither and stop in the doorway itself, between the room and the hall, which is where you have actually been living since a door shut on your wife.

nodes.text: You own everything the window shows you: the lake, the shoreline, the road in, and the men standing along it. The house contains a sister, a housekeeper, and a telephone. Anthony sings in Palermo and does not write to you. Every evening you take the chair with the good whisky and the ledgers, upright and formal and entirely correct, a king in a country with no subjects left in it.

You take a house outside Corleone with a wall around it and orange trees inside the wall, and you read the same psalm every morning before the heat comes up. The old men touch their hats to the American. You keep your coat buttoned in June. Nothing thaws: not the hands, not the voice, not the thing that shut on a road in Sicily. The trees go on regardless. They were never yours to disappoint.

You get her face in the closing doorway for the rest of your life. At odd hours, in the middle of somebody's sentence, over the top of a menu. Not the hearings, not the shouting in the hotel, not the boat going out at dusk. Just a woman holding a drink she made for you, watching a door swing shut. You will be looking at it when you go. You are looking at it right now.
